newsitem.title: BELGIUM: 11 African freighters seek exemption from new Ostend.
newsitem.headline: 11 African freighters seek exemption from new Ostend.

text.p: Only 11 freighter aircraft out of 43 African-based freighters using Belgium's Ostend airport are seeking an exemption from tougher European Union rules for older and noiser Chapter 2 aircraft, a Belgian air industry official said.
The 11 freighters will be able to fly until the year 2002 if they obtain the exemption, Paul van Krenkelsven, commercial adviser to both Ostend and Antwerp airports told Reuters.
Otherwise they will be banned under an EU directive, which stated that all aircraft older than 28 years must leave the airport by January 1, 1998.

Air cargo industry sources suggest that the airport could lose up to half of its freight if the aircraft do not get an exemption; and if the freighters still chose to fly into Europe, the country appearing to be most likely to win the traffic is Romania, they said.
The older, noisier aircraft are being discouraged from European airports because of their noise impact on surrounding areas.
Exemptions are available for aircraft from developing African countries or if airlines have a history of calling at an airport for at least four years.
In 1996, Ostend Airport handled nearly 92,000 tonnes of cargo, with up to six freighter flights a day using the airport.
An Ostend airport spokeswoman said that many of the carriers are not in a position to buy new aircraft able to meet the quieter, Stage 3, standards.

Many of the aircraft flying into Ostend fit into the noisy Chapter 2 aircraft category. Boeing 707, Douglas DC-8, Ilyushin IL 76 and Antonov AN-12 aircraft were the most common users of the airport in 1996.

An Ostend airport group, including cargo handler Belgavia, the local chamber of commerce, the airport authority national airline, Sabena and others, is appealing to the Belgian government over the directive's impact.
Of the 100 companies using the airport, the main countries of orgin or destination were Egypt, the UK, C.I.S, Senegal and Nigeria last year.
Vegetables, fruit, flowers, textiles, animals, cigarettes and machine parts made up the most of the shipments, an official report shows.

As noise regulations tightened in the Netherlands many aircraft that had been calling at Dutch airports such as Amsterdam and Maastricht airports, left for Ostend where the noise regulations have not been so strict.
